label: The Uyghur & Qara-Khitai Steppe
pitch:
Between the Göktürks and Genghis Khan lies the steppe's forgotten half-millennium. The Uyghurs overthrew the Turks in 744, rescued the Tang dynasty from collapse and walked away as its creditor, and made a Persian gnostic religion — Manichaeism — their state faith. Destroyed in a single year by the Kyrgyz in 840, they reinvented themselves as settled Buddhist oasis merchants of the Silk Road, while their Karluk cousins became the first Turkic Muslims. Then a Buddhist Khitan refugee dynasty, the Qara-Khitai, fled China and ended up ruling Muslim Central Asia — until the Mongols swallowed it all.

🔑 Key Facts:
• The Uyghur intervention in the An Lushan rebellion (755–763) inverted the steppe–China balance: China paid the nomads.
• Bögü Khan's conversion to Manichaeism (762) is the only case of a steppe empire adopting a literate missionary religion of the settled world.
• The Kingdom of Qocho turned a destroyed nomad khaganate into a multireligious agrarian trade state — and gave the Mongols their script and scribes.
• Yelü Dashi's Qara-Khitai crushed the Seljuk sultan at Qatwan (1141), the battle that seeded Europe's 'Prester John' legend.

🤔 Why It Matters: This is the bridge the reader is missing — how the Turkic world became literate, urban, and Muslim, and how the administrative DNA the Mongol Empire ran on was Uyghur.

🎲 Wild Card: Küchlüg, a Naiman prince and Christian, usurped the throne of a Buddhist empire and then persecuted its Muslim majority — until a Mongol general had him hunted down in 1218 and his head paraded through the cities he had oppressed.

spans.label: The Uyghur Khaganate
spans.description: From the overthrow of the Second Turkic Khaganate to the Kyrgyz sack of Ordu-Baliq — a literate, Manichaean steppe empire that lived off the Tang silk trade.

spans.label: The Manichaean State
spans.description: Bögü Khan's adoption of Manichaeism and the Sogdian-influenced, urban, scribal character of the Uyghur elite.

spans.label: The Oasis Kingdoms
spans.description: The Ganzhou and Qocho Uyghur states: nomads turned settled Buddhist Silk Road merchants of the Tarim.

spans.label: The Kara-Khanid Khanate
spans.description: The first Turkic Muslim dynasty: Satuq Bughra Khan's conversion, the conquest of Transoxiana, and the birth of Turkic-Islamic literature.

spans.label: The Qara-Khitai
spans.description: Yelü Dashi's Western Liao: a Chinese-Buddhist refugee dynasty ruling a Muslim Central Asia by tolerant indirect rule.

spans.label: The Eve of the Mongols
spans.description: Küchlüg's usurpation, Genghis Khan's unification of the steppe, and the absorption of the Uyghur and Qara-Khitai worlds into the Mongol Empire.

events.label: The Three-Tribe Revolt Against the Türks
events.description: The Uyghur, Karluk, and Basmyl tribes rose together against the failing Second Turkic Khaganate, beginning the war that would end Göktürk power on the Orkhon.

events.label: Qutlugh Bilge Köl Founds the Uyghur Khaganate
events.description: Qutlugh Bilge Köl Kaghan defeated the last Göktürk ruler and proclaimed the Uyghur Khaganate, making the Uyghurs masters of the eastern steppe.

events.label: Death of the Last Eastern Türk Qaghan
events.description: Özmiş Qaghan, the last ruler of the Göktürk line, was killed and his head sent to the Tang court — the formal extinction of the empire the Uyghurs replaced.

events.label: Accession of Bayanchur Khan
events.description: El Etmish Bilge Qaghan, known as Bayanchur or Moyun Chur, took the throne and expanded the khaganate to its greatest steppe extent.

events.label: Construction of Ordu-Baliq
events.description: The Uyghurs built a walled imperial capital, Ordu-Baliq (Karabalgasun), on the Orkhon River — a fortified, planned city, rare for a nomad empire.

events.label: The Shine Usu and Tariat Inscriptions
events.description: Bayanchur Khan recorded his campaigns and the founding of the khaganate in Old Turkic runic inscriptions, the chief native source for early Uyghur history.

events.label: The Battle of Talas
events.description: When the Karluks defected mid-battle, an Abbasid army defeated the Tang at Talas — a turning point that pulled the western steppe toward the Islamic world.

events.label: Sogdian Merchants Enter Uyghur Service
events.description: Sogdian traders and scribes from the Silk Road oases became the khaganate's diplomats, financiers, and administrators, tying the nomad state to settled commerce.

events.label: The An Lushan Rebellion Erupts
events.description: An Lushan's revolt nearly destroyed the Tang dynasty, emptying north China of order and forcing the emperor to flee — and to look to the steppe for rescue.

events.label: Tang Appeals to the Uyghurs for Aid
events.description: The cornered Tang court bought Uyghur cavalry with the promise of plunder and tribute, beginning the relationship that would invert the steppe–China order.

events.label: Uyghurs Recapture Chang'an and Luoyang
events.description: Uyghur horsemen spearheaded the reconquest of both Tang capitals, with Luoyang handed over to a brutal three-day sack as the agreed price.

events.label: Princess Ningguo Married to the Kaghan
events.description: The Tang sent a true imperial princess to the Uyghur ruler — a humiliating reversal of the usual direction of steppe–China marriage diplomacy.

events.label: The Horse-and-Silk Trade
events.description: The Uyghurs forced the Tang into a fixed exchange of broken-down steppe horses for vast quantities of silk, draining the Chinese treasury for decades.

events.label: Bögü Khan's Second Intervention
events.description: Tengri Bögü Khan led a fresh Uyghur army into China, retook Luoyang from rebel remnants, and met the Sogdian Manichaean priests who would change his court.

events.label: Bögü Khan Converts to Manichaeism
events.description: Bögü Khan adopted Manichaeism, a dualist Persian religion of the settled world, after debating with Sogdian Electi in occupied Luoyang.

events.label: Manichaeism Becomes the State Religion
events.description: The khaganate made Manichaeism official — the only steppe empire ever to take a literate, missionary, scriptural faith of the agrarian world as its state religion.

events.label: Manichaean Monasteries at Ordu-Baliq
events.description: Manichaean clergy, temples, and a scriptorium were established in the Uyghur capital, giving the nomad elite a resident literate priesthood.

events.label: The Old Uyghur Alphabet
events.description: The Uyghurs adapted the Sogdian script into the Old Uyghur alphabet, the writing system later borrowed by the Mongols and Manchus.

events.label: The Karabalgasun Trilingual Inscription
events.description: A great stele at the capital recorded Uyghur history and the Manichaean conversion in Old Turkic, Sogdian, and Chinese — a monument to a deliberately multilingual state.

events.label: Sogdian Advisers Dominate the Court
events.description: Manichaean Sogdians ran Uyghur diplomacy and finance, pushing aggressive trade demands on China and steering the khaganate's foreign policy.

events.label: Anti-Uyghur Backlash at the Tang Court
events.description: After Bögü Khan's death, resentment of Uyghur arrogance and the ruinous trade burst into massacres of Uyghur and Sogdian merchants in China.

events.label: Assassination of Bögü Khan
events.description: Bögü Khan was killed by his minister Tun Bagha Tarkhan in a coup that checked the Manichaean-Sogdian war party but kept the religion.

events.label: The Kaghan Builds in Stone and Silk
events.description: Arab and Chinese visitors described Ordu-Baliq's golden tent, fortified walls, and markets — the wealth a nomad empire accumulated by taxing trade.

events.label: Succession Wars Weaken the Khaganate
events.description: A run of short reigns and assassinated kaghans hollowed out central authority in the decades before the collapse.

events.label: The Great Steppe Famine
events.description: A catastrophic winter killed the herds and brought epidemic and starvation, fatally weakening the khaganate just before the Kyrgyz attack.

events.label: A Rebel General Invites the Kyrgyz
events.description: The disaffected commander Külüg Bagha defected and guided the Yenisei Kyrgyz army down onto the Orkhon heartland.

events.label: The Kyrgyz Sack Ordu-Baliq
events.description: A Kyrgyz army stormed and burned the Uyghur capital, killed the kaghan, and destroyed the khaganate in a single campaigning season.

events.label: The Uyghur Diaspora
events.description: The surviving Uyghurs scattered in three great migrations — south to the Tang frontier, west to the Gansu corridor, and southwest to the Tarim oases.

events.label: The Tang Persecute the Manichaeans
events.description: With their Uyghur protectors gone, the Manichaean church in China was crushed: temples seized, priests killed or defrocked, in a prelude to the wider Huichang persecutions.

events.label: The Kyrgyz Fail to Hold the Steppe
events.description: The Yenisei Kyrgyz looted the Orkhon but withdrew to Siberia rather than rule it, leaving a power vacuum that lasted until the Mongols.

events.label: The Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom
events.description: Uyghur refugees in the Gansu corridor founded the Ganzhou Kingdom, controlling a key Silk Road stretch between China and the Tarim.

events.label: Pugu Jun Founds the Kingdom of Qocho
events.description: A Uyghur leader took Turfan and Beshbalik and established the Kingdom of Qocho, the longest-lived and richest of the oasis Uyghur states.

events.label: The Qocho Uyghurs Turn Buddhist
events.description: In the Tarim oases the Uyghurs gradually abandoned Manichaeism for Buddhism, with a Nestorian Christian minority — a wholesale religious reinvention.

events.label: The Bezeklik Thousand Buddha Caves
events.description: Uyghur patrons filled the Bezeklik cave temples near Turfan with murals, fusing Indian, Chinese, and Iranian styles into a distinct Uyghur Buddhist art.

events.label: Old Uyghur Becomes a Literary Language
events.description: Qocho's scribes translated Buddhist and Manichaean texts into Old Uyghur, producing one of medieval Inner Asia's largest surviving literatures.

events.label: Qocho as a Silk Road Entrepôt
events.description: The oasis Uyghurs grew rich as middlemen — taxing caravans, lending capital, and supplying scribes and interpreters across the Tarim trade network.

events.label: Uyghur Block Printing
events.description: Qocho workshops printed Buddhist texts with woodblocks and movable wooden type, part of the oasis Uyghurs' deeply literate settled culture.

events.label: The Wang Yande Embassy to Qocho
events.description: A Song Chinese envoy described Qocho's irrigated fields, libraries, and Buddhist temples — an eyewitness portrait of a nomad people gone fully agrarian.

events.label: The Kara-Khanid Khanate Forms
events.description: Out of the Karluk, Yagma, and Chigil tribes a new western Turkic confederation, the Kara-Khanids, took shape around Kashgar and Balasagun.

events.label: Satuq Bughra Khan Converts to Islam
events.description: The Kara-Khanid prince Satuq Bughra Khan accepted Islam, seized power, and became the first Turkic Muslim ruler — a hinge in world history.

events.label: The Conversion of the Two Hundred Thousand Tents
events.description: Arabic sources report a mass conversion of some 200,000 Turkic households to Islam under Satuq's successors — the religious tipping point of the steppe.

events.label: The Kara-Khanids Take Bukhara
events.description: Kara-Khanid armies seized Bukhara and ended the Persian Samanid dynasty, putting Transoxiana under Turkic Muslim rule for the first time.

events.label: The Dual-Kaghanate Constitution
events.description: The Kara-Khanids ruled through a layered system of senior and junior khans over eastern and western realms — flexible, fissile, and uniquely steppe-Islamic.

events.label: Kashgar and Balasagun Rise
events.description: The Kara-Khanid capitals became centers of Turkic-Islamic architecture, madrasas, and caravan wealth on the western Silk Road.

events.label: Yusuf Khass Hajib Writes the Kutadgu Bilig
events.description: The Kutadgu Bilig, a long Turkic mirror-for-princes composed at Kashgar, was the first major literary work of Islamic Turkic civilization.

events.label: Mahmud al-Kashgari's Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk
events.description: Mahmud al-Kashgari compiled a vast Turkic-Arabic dictionary and the first known map centered on the Turkic world, preserving the language and its peoples.

events.label: The Kara-Khanids Become Seljuk Vassals
events.description: The Great Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah I forced the western Kara-Khanids into vassalage, drawing the eastern Turkic world into the wider Islamic order.

events.label: Madrasas Spread in the Eastern Turkic World
events.description: Islamic colleges, Sufi lodges, and Arabic-Persian learning took root from Kashgar to Bukhara, binding the Turks into Islamic high culture.

events.label: The Liao Dynasty Falls to the Jurchen
events.description: The Jurchen Jin destroyed the Khitan Liao empire in north China, sending a remnant of the Khitan elite fleeing west under Yelü Dashi.

events.label: Yelü Dashi's March West
events.description: With a few thousand followers Yelü Dashi crossed the steppe, gathered tribes, and seized the old Uyghur and Kara-Khanid lands of Central Asia.

events.label: Yelü Dashi Proclaimed Gurkhan
events.description: Yelü Dashi took the title Gurkhan ('khan of khans') and founded the Qara-Khitai, or Western Liao — a Chinese-Buddhist dynasty on Muslim soil.

events.label: The Battle of Qatwan
events.description: Yelü Dashi crushed the Great Seljuk sultan Sanjar near Samarkand — the largest defeat of a Muslim army in the East and the seed of Europe's Prester John legend.

events.label: A Buddhist Empire Over Muslim Subjects
events.description: The Qara-Khitai ruled a majority-Muslim Central Asia with a Chinese administrative model and conspicuous religious tolerance, taxing rather than converting.

events.label: Rule by Vassal and Tribute
events.description: The Gurkhans governed indirectly through subordinate Kara-Khanid khans, the Khwarazm-Shahs, and the Qocho idiqut, collecting tribute and hostages rather than annexing.

events.label: The Prester John Legend
events.description: Garbled news of a Christian-seeming king who had smashed a Muslim army at Qatwan reached the Crusader West as the myth of Prester John.

events.label: The Qara-Khitai Control the Silk Roads
events.description: From Balasagun the Gurkhans held the trans-Asian trade arteries, and their stable, tolerant rule is remembered as a high point for the oasis cities.

events.label: The Qocho Uyghurs Submit to the Qara-Khitai
events.description: The Buddhist Uyghur kingdom of Qocho accepted Qara-Khitai overlordship, paying tribute through a resident commissioner.

events.label: Khwarazm and the Kara-Khanids Revolt
events.description: The rising Khwarazmian Empire and restless Kara-Khanid vassals began tearing at an overstretched Qara-Khitai from the west.

events.label: Genghis Khan Destroys the Naiman
events.description: Temüjin shattered the Naiman confederation; the Naiman prince Küchlüg fled west toward the Qara-Khitai court.

events.label: Temüjin Proclaimed Genghis Khan
events.description: At a great assembly on the Onon, Temüjin was proclaimed Genghis Khan and the whole eastern steppe was unified under one ruler for the first time since the Uyghurs.

events.label: The Uyghur Idiqut Submits to Genghis Khan
events.description: Barchuq, the idiqut of Qocho, killed the Qara-Khitai resident and voluntarily submitted to the Mongols, becoming a privileged 'fifth son' of Genghis Khan.

events.label: Küchlüg Usurps the Qara-Khitai Throne
events.description: The fugitive Naiman prince Küchlüg seized the Gurkhan's throne by marriage and coup, ending the Yelü line's rule from within.

events.label: Küchlüg Persecutes the Muslims
events.description: Küchlüg, a convert to Buddhism, abandoned the dynasty's tolerance and persecuted the Muslim majority of the Tarim, turning his subjects against him.

events.label: Jebe Destroys Küchlüg
events.description: The Mongol general Jebe overran the Qara-Khitai, proclaimed religious freedom to win the population, and had Küchlüg hunted down and killed.

events.label: The Uyghurs Become the Mongols' Scribes
events.description: The Mongols adopted the Old Uyghur alphabet for their own language and staffed their new empire's chancery with literate Uyghur administrators.

events.label: Tatatonga Brings the Seal and the Script
events.description: A captured Uyghur scribe of the Naiman, Tatatonga, taught the Mongols the use of the state seal and the Uyghur script — the administrative bridge into the Mongol era.

events.label: The Tarim and Steppe Pass to the Mongols
events.description: With Qocho a willing vassal and the Qara-Khitai annexed, the entire Uyghur and Central Asian world fell into the Mongol Empire, closing the post-Türk interregnum.

events.label: The Manichaean Hymnbook of Qocho
events.description: The Mahrnamag and other illuminated Manichaean manuscripts from Qocho preserve the only substantial surviving Manichaean art and liturgy in the world.

events.label: Uyghur Cavalry in the Tang Civil Wars
events.description: Uyghur mercenary armies repeatedly re-entered China through the 760s, propping up and pressuring the Tang in exchange for ever-larger payments.

events.label: The Idiqut Title and the Qocho Court
events.description: Qocho's rulers took the title idiqut and built a Chinese-style bureaucratic court over an irrigated agrarian economy, the antithesis of the old khaganate.

events.label: Nestorian Christianity in the Tarim
events.description: The Church of the East maintained bishoprics and monasteries among the Uyghurs of Qocho, part of the oasis world's dense religious pluralism.

events.label: The Karluk Migration to Semirechye
events.description: The Karluks seized the Western Türk lands around the Ili and Chu valleys, founding the western Turkic base from which the Kara-Khanids would later grow.

events.label: The Uyghurs Tax the Caravans
events.description: At their height the khaganate's wealth rested less on plunder than on protecting and taxing the Sogdian Silk Road traffic through its territory.

events.label: Mahmud al-Kashgari Maps the Turkic World
events.description: Al-Kashgari's circular world map, centered on Balasagun, is the earliest surviving map drawn from a Turkic point of view.

events.label: The Western Kara-Khanids Under the Seljuks
events.description: Sanjar's Seljuks dominated the western Kara-Khanid khans until Qatwan, when the Qara-Khitai displaced Seljuk power east of the Oxus.

events.label: The Gurkhan's Tolerant Tax State
events.description: Contemporaries praised Qara-Khitai justice: light, regular taxation, no forced conversion, and protection of merchants — rare stability before the Mongol storm.

events.label: The Khwarazm-Shah Breaks Free
events.description: Ala ad-Din Muhammad of Khwarazm defeated Qara-Khitai forces and threw off tribute, hastening the dynasty's collapse just as Küchlüg seized its center.

events.label: The Steppe's Literate Memory
events.description: The Kutadgu Bilig and the Dīwān together announced that the Turks now had their own Islamic literary civilization, not merely a borrowed one.

events.label: Uyghur Loanwords Enter Mongol Statecraft
events.description: Mongol terms for writing, taxation, and office were borrowed wholesale from Uyghur, the clearest proof that the Mongol Empire ran on Uyghur administrative DNA.

events.label: Bayanchur's Sogdian City-Builders
events.description: Bayanchur Khan settled Sogdian and Chinese craftsmen to build the fortress-town of Bay Baliq on the Selenga — nomads commissioning a city.

events.label: The Uyghur Princesses of the Tang
events.description: The Tang sent Princess Taihe to the Uyghur kaghan; her ordeal and rescue after the 840 collapse became a famous tale of the steppe–China bond.

events.label: The Qocho Uyghurs Translate the Buddhist Canon
events.description: Qocho's monasteries rendered Sanskrit, Tocharian, and Chinese scriptures into Old Uyghur, making it a major language of Central Asian Buddhism.

events.label: Satuq Bughra Khan's Holy War
events.description: Satuq's seizure of Kashgar was framed as a war of Islam against the pagan Turks, casting the Kara-Khanid conversion as a religious revolution.

events.label: Yelü Dashi's Chinese Institutions
events.description: The Gurkhan kept Liao reign-titles, a Chinese-style chancery, and centralized salaried officials rather than granting nomadic appanages — a transplanted Chinese state.

events.label: The Uyghur–Tang Alliance of 744
events.description: Qutlugh Bilge Köl allied with the Tang against the Basmyl and the last Türks, securing Chinese recognition for the new khaganate at its birth.

events.label: The Toquz Oghuz Tribal Order
events.description: The khaganate was built on the Toquz Oghuz, a confederation of nine core tribes under the ruling Yaglakar clan — the political skeleton of Uyghur power.

events.label: The Uyghur Heavy Cavalry
events.description: Uyghur armies fielded armored lancers in disciplined tümen formations, the striking force that made them indispensable to the Tang.

events.label: The First Horse-Market Agreement
events.description: An early fixed-rate exchange of Uyghur horses for Tang silk was negotiated, the template for the trade that would later bleed the Chinese treasury.

events.label: Bay Baliq, the Town on the Selenga
events.description: Sogdian and Chinese craftsmen built Bayanchur Khan a second walled town, Bay Baliq, evidence of a deliberate Uyghur turn toward urban settlement.

events.label: Manichaean Astronomy at the Court
events.description: Manichaean and Sogdian clergy brought calendrical and astronomical learning to Ordu-Baliq, giving the khaganate a literate scientific elite.

events.label: Princess Taihe Sent to the Kaghan
events.description: The Tang dispatched Princess Taihe to the Uyghur ruler in a lavish embassy, the last great marriage-alliance before the collapse.

events.label: The Regicide Cycle
events.description: Kaghan Zhaoli was murdered by his own ministers, one of a run of palace killings that gutted Uyghur central authority in the 830s.

events.label: Plague Among the Herds
events.description: Disease swept the Uyghur horse and sheep herds just before the killing winter, compounding the subsistence crisis that doomed the khaganate.

events.label: The Golden Tent Burned
events.description: The Kyrgyz killed the last kaghan, Hesa, and burned the royal golden tent — the symbolic end of the Uyghur imperial line on the Orkhon.

events.label: The Southern Migration Destroyed
events.description: The Uyghur remnant that fled toward the Tang frontier was attacked and broken by Chinese armies at the Battle of Shahu, ending hopes of a restoration.

events.label: The Orkhon Falls Silent
events.description: For the first time in three centuries no steppe empire ruled from the Orkhon; the imperial heartland lay empty until Genghis Khan in 1206.

events.label: The Karez Irrigation of Turfan
events.description: The Qocho Uyghurs maintained and extended the karez underground canal system, turning the Turfan depression into productive farmland.

events.label: The Ruins of Gaochang
events.description: The Uyghur capital of Qocho at Gaochang grew into a great mud-brick city of temples and monasteries whose ruins still stand near Turfan.

events.label: The Tomb of Satuq Bughra Khan
events.description: The shrine of the first Muslim Turkic ruler at Artush became a pilgrimage center, anchoring the memory of the Kara-Khanid conversion.

events.label: The Ortoq Merchant Partnerships
events.description: Uyghur and Central Asian traders ran ortoq capital-pooling partnerships, a commercial institution the Mongols later adopted empire-wide as the ortogh.

events.label: Yelü Dashi, the Scholar-Prince
events.description: Yelü Dashi was a jinshi-degree Khitan aristocrat steeped in Chinese letters, the unlikely refugee who would carry a Chinese state into Muslim Asia.

events.label: The Mausoleum of Yusuf Khass Hajib
events.description: The poet of the Kutadgu Bilig was honored with a tomb at Kashgar that remains a monument to the birth of Turkic-Islamic literature.

events.label: Uyghur Scribes Staff the Mongol Chancery
events.description: Literate Qocho Uyghurs became the clerks, tutors, and tax-officials of the early Mongol Empire, transmitting settled statecraft to the conquerors.

events.label: The Idiqut Honored as Genghis Khan's Fifth Son
events.description: Barchuq the idiqut was rewarded for early submission with a Mongol princess and the rank of a son of Genghis Khan — the Uyghurs' privileged place in the new order.
